paragraphs: Put on headphones and type while listening to each dictated passage. Rewind unclear terms and verify them in medical dictionaries. Arrange the history of present illness, physical examination, and diagnosis in standard templates. Highlight contradictions for clinician confirmation. Before leaving, encrypt and archive completed records for quality-control sampling.

In short, transcriptionists turn dictated medical records into text. They listen and transcribe, verify terminology and drug names, standardize formatting, flag contradictions, proofread completed documents, and encrypt archives. Accuracy is central because one incorrect word can affect treatment.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 43,900 medical transcriptionists were employed in 2024, declining to a projected 41,800 by 2034. That represents roughly 2,100 fewer jobs, with about 7,400 openings per year and median annual pay of approximately $37,500 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI is replacing medical transcriptionists more thoroughly than it replaces most occupations. Speech recognition and medical large language models turn dictation directly into drafts, sharply reducing demand for manual transcription. People are still needed for quality control, terminology verification, and privacy safeguards. The path forward is not continued dictation work, but movement into health-record quality control, coding, and data governance.
